41.event_title: Young Anton Chekhov supports his family
41.event: When Anton Chekhov's father went bankrupt and, facing prison, moved the family to Moscow, the teenage Anton stayed behind in Taganrog from 1876 to 1879, earning his living as a tutor and sending money to his parents. After entering the medical faculty of Moscow University in 1879, where the family lived in poverty, he supported them by writing large numbers of comic stories and sketches for humorous magazines while he studied.
41.explanation: Before he became one of the world's great writers, Chekhov's early work was driven by the need to keep his parents and siblings afloat.
41.tie_back: The kural defines the true householder as the steady support of those who depend on him, and the young Chekhov became the mainstay of his parents and siblings through honest work.
41._accuracy_note: A good picture of one person becoming the support of his dependants, though Chekhov was a son supporting his family rather than a married householder as the kural envisages.

42.event_title: Emperor Harsha's five-yearly gift-giving at Prayag
42.event: Harsha, who ruled much of northern India from 606 to 647, held a great gathering every five years at Prayag, where the Ganges and Yamuna meet. The Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang, who travelled in India between 629 and 645, recorded the king's generosity there, describing how he gave gifts and donations to scholars and ascetics. At these ceremonies of giving, most of the wealth gathered over the previous five years was given away in charity.
42.explanation: Harsha's assemblies became one of the most celebrated examples of royal charity in early Indian history, preserved by an eyewitness from another land.
42.tie_back: The kural names the householder as the support of those who have renounced the world and of the destitute, and Harsha's gifts to ascetics and to the needy at Prayag show such support given on a grand scale.
42._accuracy_note: Matches the support of renunciants and the needy well, but a king's public charity is not quite the ordinary householder's duty, and the kural's third group, the dead, is not shown.

43.event_title: UNESCO recognises Mexico's Day of the Dead
43.event: In 2003 UNESCO proclaimed the indigenous festivity dedicated to the dead, as practised in Mexico, a masterpiece of humanity's intangible heritage, and in 2008 inscribed it on its Representative List. At the end of October and start of November, families lay flower petals and candles along the path from the cemetery to their homes, prepare the favourite dishes of departed relatives, and place them with offerings on home altars and graves. The custom blends pre-Hispanic rites with the Catholic feasts of All Saints and All Souls.
43.explanation: The festival shows a whole society setting aside time each year to honour its ancestors through family gatherings, shared food and religious observance.
43.tie_back: The kural lists the householder's duty to the departed ancestors, the gods, kin and others, and the Day of the Dead joins remembrance of ancestors, worship and family feasting in a single household observance.
43._accuracy_note: Partial fit: it shows several of the kural's five claims (ancestors, the divine, kin) honoured together, but guests and care of oneself are not prominent, and it is a recurring custom rather than a single act.

44.event_title: Mitsui Takatoshi opens the Echigoya shop
44.event: Mitsui Takatoshi, a merchant from Matsusaka who had earlier returned home to care for his mother, opened a textile shop called Echigoya in Edo in 1673. The shop became known for selling for cash at fixed prices with no mark-ups, as its signboards announced, and it grew into the largest textile store of the Edo period. Echigoya became the forerunner of the Mitsukoshi department store, and the family's money-exchange business led eventually to the modern Mitsui group.
44.explanation: Mitsui's plain, fair pricing helped build one of the longest-lasting family enterprises in the world.
44.tie_back: The kural promises that a household that earns without blame will never see its line fail, and the Mitsui name, founded on openly fair dealing, has continued for more than three centuries.
44._accuracy_note: Partial fit: blameless earning and lasting continuity are shown, but the kural's second condition, sharing one's food before eating, is not, and a business line is not the same as a family lineage.

45.event_title: The von Trapp family leaves Nazi-annexed Austria
45.place: Salzburg, Austria, to Stowe, Vermont, United States
45.event: The von Trapps of Salzburg had turned their family love of singing into a professional choir after losing most of their wealth when their bank failed in the early 1930s. After Nazi Germany annexed Austria in 1938, Georg von Trapp refused to fly the Nazi flag on their house, declined a naval command and turned down a request for the family to sing at Hitler's birthday party. Unwilling to compromise their principles, the family left Austria by train for Italy and went on to America, where they toured as the Trapp Family Singers and settled on a farm in Stowe, Vermont.
45.explanation: The real von Trapps chose to give up home and possessions together rather than serve a regime they abhorred, and they rebuilt their life as a family.
45.tie_back: The kural says that love and virtue are both the character and the reward of domestic life, and the von Trapps, bound by affection and holding to principle, found their wealth in each other rather than in what they left behind.
45._accuracy_note: Shows a household held together by love and principle, though the kural's claim that these are their own reward is an inner truth that the family's later success does not by itself prove.

46.event_title: Martin Luther marries Katharina von Bora
46.event: Martin Luther, a former Augustinian friar, married Katharina von Bora, a former Cistercian nun who had left her convent in 1523, on 13 June 1525. According to Britannica, Luther was convinced that marriage was an honourable order of creation and chose to take a public stand against clerical celibacy. The couple raised six children in the former monastery building in Wittenberg, where Katharina ran the household and its finances, which also came to include her relative, six of Luther's sister's children and student lodgers.
46.explanation: Luther's marriage made the family home of a former monk a model of married life that many later clergy followed.
46.tie_back: The kural asks what more a person could gain by another path if household life is lived in virtue, and Luther left the monastic path to make a household the setting of his religious life.
46._accuracy_note: A direct historical instance of choosing household life over the renunciant path, though the religious meaning of this choice is understood differently by different Christian traditions.

47.event_title: Guru Nanak settles as a farmer at Kartarpur
47.event: After about twenty years of travel preaching his message, Guru Nanak settled again with his family in the Punjab, became a farmer and established the village of Kartarpur. Disciples gathered around him in a community of work and worship, and he devoted the last twenty years of his life to shaping the first Sikh community there. Before his death in 1539 he appointed a faithful follower, Guru Angad, as his successor.
47.explanation: The founder of Sikhism chose to lead his community as a working family man rather than as a wandering ascetic, setting a pattern for the faith that followed.
47.tie_back: The kural says one who lives household life as it should be lived stands foremost among all who strive, and Guru Nanak made a farming family life the base from which he guided his followers.
47._accuracy_note: A strong fit for the householder's life placed at the head of spiritual striving, coming from a tradition that itself honours the householder path.

48.event: At the rectory in Epworth, Susanna Wesley raised the ten of her nineteen children who survived infancy and taught them herself on a strict daily timetable, with lessons from nine to noon and two to five, girls as well as boys learning to read from the age of five, and prayers at rising and bedtime. During her husband's long absences she also read prayers and sermons to neighbours at the rectory, gatherings that at one time drew around 200 people. Her sons John and Charles Wesley went on to found the Methodist movement, and she is often called the Mother of Methodism.
48.explanation: Susanna Wesley's ordered, devout household shaped two of the most influential religious leaders of the eighteenth century and reached out to her whole village.
48.tie_back: The kural praises a household that keeps others on the right path while never slipping itself as stronger than the austerities of ascetics, and Susanna Wesley's home guided her children and neighbours alike.
48._accuracy_note: A good example of a household leading others on the right path; the comparison with ascetic austerity is the kural's own judgement and not something the event can prove.

49.event_title: Father Damien serves the Hansen's disease settlement on Molokai
49.place: Kalawao, Kalaupapa Peninsula, Molokai, Kingdom of Hawaii (now Hawaii, United States)
49.event: In 1873 Father Damien, a Belgian Catholic priest, went to the isolated settlement at Kalawao on Molokai, where the Hawaiian government sent people with Hansen's disease (leprosy). He helped build about 300 of the settlement's 325 buildings, including homes and churches, constructed water lines and roads, administered medicine, improved food supplies and founded two orphanages. After twelve years he contracted the disease himself, and he died there on 15 April 1889 after sixteen years of voluntary service.
49.explanation: Damien's life of celibate service among people shunned by society won worldwide admiration even in his own lifetime, and he was later declared a saint.
49.tie_back: The kural concedes that the renunciant path is also good if no one has cause to reproach it, and Damien's selfless life among the outcast is a renunciant life that drew praise rather than reproach.
49._accuracy_note: Illustrates the second half of the kural, a blameless renunciant life, but not its main claim that household life is virtue itself.

50.event_title: Imhotep, builder of the Step Pyramid, is later worshipped as a god
50.date: c. 27th century BCE; worshipped in the Late Period
50.event: Imhotep was a high official of King Djoser of Egypt's Third Dynasty; his name and titles are carved on the base of a statue of the king, and he is credited with designing Djoser's Step Pyramid at Saqqara, Egypt's first monumental structure in stone. His memory lasted for millennia: by the New Kingdom he was listed among the wise men of the past and revered as patron of scribes, and in the Late Period he was worshipped as a god of medicine and son of the god Ptah, later identified by the Greeks with Asklepios.
50.explanation: Imhotep is one of very few people in Egyptian history known to have been raised to divine status after death, purely through the regard in which his life and wisdom were held.
50.tie_back: The kural says one who lives on earth as one ought will be counted among the gods in the sky, and Imhotep, a human official remembered for wisdom and achievement, was literally later counted among Egypt's gods.
50._accuracy_note: Next-best: a real person was literally counted among the gods, but little is known of how Imhotep lived, so the kural's link between right living and this honour cannot be shown.
